title: Zwingli's sausages
hook: in Zurich, eating sausages in Lent starts a reformation

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luther's Small Catechism, a thin book for teaching at home. Your line was what does this mean? Which familiar phrase did you finally stop and open? Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

The presses at a print shop in Zurich have been running hard. The printer, a man named Christoph Froschauer, has a big job due, and his workers are worn out. It's Lent, the season before Easter when the church of their day forbids meat. And at a meal in the printer's house, the story goes, someone brings out sausages. They're cut up and shared around the table. A local priest is in the room. His name is Huldrych Zwingli. Word gets out, the city council gets involved, and a plate of sausages turns into a public question about the whole church. Today: Zwingli's sausages.

Here's the odd part. By the usual account, Zwingli didn't eat any. He sat at the table and let it happen. But when the eaters were accused, he stood up for them, and preached a sermon later printed as On the Choice and Freedom of Foods. His argument went to the Bible. Where, he asked, does scripture command this? He pointed to Paul, who writes in the King James Bible: "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday." Fasting, Zwingli said, can be a good thing. Anyone who wants to fast in Lent should be free to. But it shouldn't be a law that binds every conscience under threat of punishment. That's the hinge. Not a rule against fasting. A question about who gets to make the rule. And once Zurich started asking that question about sausages, it started asking it about everything else too, until the city's church was reshaped around preaching from scripture. Paul has a second line that cuts both ways, and it's worth holding next to the first. "Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth." The eater shouldn't sneer. The faster shouldn't judge. Christians today keep Lent in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox Christians keep the Lenten fast together, as a discipline of the whole church. Some Protestant Christians fast by choice, or give something up. Underneath all of it is the question Zwingli raised, and it's an honest one: why do we do this?
screen: `LET NO MAN JUDGE YOU IN MEAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: question one rule you keep without thinking. It might be a religious habit, a family custom, a way things are always done at work. Bring it to mind. Then ask Zwingli's question, gently: why do we do this? Look for the reason. Sometimes there's a good one, and the rule may mean more than it did a minute ago. Sometimes you'll find it's just habit. Either way, you'll know. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom about it. If you don't, just hold the rule up to the light for a while. The bell holds the time.
Zwingli's sausages. A meal in Lent in a Zurich print shop that Zwingli defended, and a question about rules that reshaped a city's church.
Your line: why do we do this? Today, ask it once out loud about something you do together with others, and listen to the answer before you change anything. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians keep set fasts in Lent, such as abstaining from meat on certain days; some Protestant Christians fast or give something up by personal choice during Lent.

fork.setup: you're Zwingli, a priest in Zurich. at a printer's table in Lent, sausages are passed around. what do you do?

don't eat, but defend the eaters from the pulpit.

fork.reveal: by the usual account he didn't eat, then preached that fasting should be free and not forced, and the question spread through Zurich.

trapdoor: what you thought: a funny story about a priest and some sausages.
what it means: a meal in Lent that raised the question of who gets to make rules for the church.
what a scholar hears: Zwingli's sermon on the freedom of foods argued from scripture, and Zurich's reformation grew out of that argument about authority.
